content.headline: Building from the edge can be an advantage.
content.lead: I am a Faroese software engineer and entrepreneur. My work sits where technology, learning, business and institution-building meet.
body: I have spent my career turning difficult systems into things people can understand and use: simulation-based learning, data-rich web applications, software companies and, now, a durable memory layer for human and AI collaboration.

Today I lead Usable, chair the board of the University of the Faroe Islands and Ocean Rainforest, and continue selected work through Tøkni. The common thread is capacity: helping people, organisations and small communities act with more knowledge and a longer horizon.
This site is where I write in my own voice about what we are learning along the way.
principles: Context compounds when it is kept alive.
Small places can build globally useful things.
Technology matters most when it strengthens human judgement.
Institutions deserve the same care as products.

pages.title: The Faroe Islands’ AI strategy needs a living memory

content.title: The Faroe Islands’ AI strategy needs a living memory
content.summary: The pre-study is complete and the action plan is taking shape. The next challenge is to keep what the project learns retrievable—and turn that memory into a useful public record.
content.bodyMarkdown:
The question I hear most often about the Faroese AI strategy is a simple one: where are we now?

The short answer is that the pre-study is finished and the real action-plan work is under way. The harder answer is that a national strategy is not one document moving neatly from draft to publication. It is a growing body of evidence, workshop findings, choices, objections, responsibilities and revisions.

If that knowledge cannot be retrieved, the project will repeatedly lose its own context. If it cannot be communicated, the public will only see occasional announcements rather than the work itself.

That is why I increasingly think about the project as two connected systems: an organisational memory in [Usable](https://usable.dev), and a public operating surface at [vitliki.talgildu.fo](https://vitliki.talgildu.fo/).

## Where the work stands

The preparatory work was [commissioned in October 2025](https://www.talgildu.fo/talgildu-foeroyar/a-breddanum/skjoetil-settur-a-almenna-nytslu-av-vitliki). Flowcore led the pre-study with Vitlíkisstovan as subcontractor. The assignment was to formulate a vision, gather contributions from institutions and other stakeholders, learn from neighbouring countries and help shape recommendations to the Government.

From November through January, a series of workshops examined six connected areas: skills and understanding, public services, business competitiveness, the Faroese language, technical infrastructure, and ethics. The point was not merely to collect opinions. It was to identify uses, obstacles, priorities and recommendations from people who know the affected parts of society.

The pre-study was completed in March, published online in April and [handed to the Minister of Finance in May](https://www.talgildu.fo/talgildu-foeroyar/a-breddanum/forkanning-um-vitliki-handad-klart-at-fara-undir-heildaraetlan). Its central direction is now public: the Faroe Islands should show how a small society can use AI responsibly to strengthen its people, language and economy.

On 6 May, around 100 people gathered in Smæran to [launch the action-plan phase](https://vitliki.talgildu.fo/pages/blog/posts/heildaraetlanin-skotin-i-gongd/index.html). The task now is to turn the vision and recommendations into concrete initiatives with ownership and funding, ready for the 2027 budget process. The public site describes the current work as continued stakeholder input, learning from other—especially Nordic—countries, and translating the pre-study into action.

So the project is no longer asking only, “What should the Faroese approach to AI be?” It is asking, “What will we do, who will own it, and how will it be financed?”

## What the public site already does well

[vitliki.talgildu.fo](https://vitliki.talgildu.fo/) has become a useful record of the first phase. The pre-study is available as a report and in an English web version. The workshop programme and summaries show which questions were asked and which parts of society were invited into the process. The launch article includes presentations, participation results and the questions raised from the room.

That is more valuable than a polished announcement with no evidence behind it. A reader can follow the movement from workshops to report to action-plan work. The site also communicates the three main pillars clearly—people, language and economy—and keeps international learning visible alongside local participation.

The limitation is freshness. As I write this on 13 August, the latest item in the public news stream is the launch on 6 May. The homepage says that work is happening now, but it does not yet let a reader follow that work in a structured way.

The gap is not necessarily inactivity. It is a lag between the project’s working memory and its published record.

## The organisational memory underneath

A project like this produces knowledge faster than it produces reports. There are source documents, workshop notes, research, alternative formulations, meeting outcomes, open questions and reasons why one proposal replaced another. Much of the value lies in those connections.

We now have a dedicated Vitlikisvitan workspace in Usable with curated material from both the pre-study and the main action-plan project. The important word is not storage. It is retrieval.

When a new question appears, a person or an AI agent should be able to find the relevant history: What did the language workshop conclude? Which assumption came from international research? Has an initiative already been proposed? Who challenged it? What evidence changed the direction? Which version is current?

A folder can preserve files. A living organisational memory should help the next person recover the reasoning across them.

That does not make Usable an authority, and it does not mean internal notes should automatically become public. The repository, approved documents, named decision-makers and current project evidence remain the sources of operational truth. Some material is preliminary or sensitive. Some conclusions become stale. Every retrieval still needs provenance, status and human judgement.

The useful loop is therefore:

> capture the source → retrieve the relevant context → decide → verify → publish what is approved → write the outcome back

The final step matters. Without it, each workshop, decision or public update becomes another endpoint. With it, the project can accumulate knowledge instead of merely accumulating documents.

## From archive to public operating surface

The public site and the internal memory should do different jobs. Usable can hold the detailed evidence and working context. The public site should turn the approved part of that knowledge into something citizens can understand and follow.

In practice, I would like the site to show more than a sequence of news posts. It should say what phase the work is in, when that status was last reviewed and what comes next. Each initiative should eventually have a visible status, owner, next milestone and supporting sources. Important changes should remain traceable instead of silently replacing yesterday’s version. Open questions should be clearly separated from confirmed decisions.

This would make the site less like a campaign page and more like the public home of the strategy: a place to understand the direction, inspect progress and know where participation is still possible.

It would also make communication easier to sustain. A meeting outcome recorded with a clear owner, source and public status can become a short update. A changed initiative can update both its own page and a monthly progress note. A completed pilot can become a case with evidence, safeguards and reusable learning. The publishing process starts from retrievable knowledge rather than from an empty page.

## The strategy should practise what it recommends

The Faroese AI strategy will make claims about how institutions should use AI responsibly. The strategy project itself is an opportunity to demonstrate that practice.

AI can help retrieve context across a long-running project, compare new proposals with earlier evidence and prepare clearer public explanations. But it should do so inside a governed process where people can inspect the sources, correct the record and decide what becomes official.

For a small society, continuity matters. We cannot afford to lose important reasoning every time a consultant leaves, a working group changes or a new tool arrives. We also cannot expect public trust if only the final recommendation is visible and the path towards it disappears.

The work now is to produce an ambitious, actionable plan for the 2027 budget. Alongside that, we should build the memory and publishing discipline that allow the plan to keep learning after it is launched.

The public can already see the foundation at vitliki.talgildu.fo. The next step is to make the living work easier to follow—and to make sure the knowledge behind it remains available for the next decision, not trapped in the last meeting or the last AI conversation.

pages.title: Claude and Codex Can’t Talk to Each Other. Usable Let Them Collaborate Anyway.

content.title: Claude and Codex Can’t Talk to Each Other. Usable Let Them Collaborate Anyway.
content.summary: What happened when I gave two otherwise isolated AI coding toolsets the same durable project memory.

heroImage.alt: Usable native apps for iOS and Android showing an answer grounded in shared workspace fragments

content.bodyMarkdown:
I started on Thursday morning, using Claude to build native iOS and Android applications for [Usable](https://usable.dev).

By this weekend, the apps had become substantial. They had authentication, workspaces, chat, search, offline support, push notifications, sharing, store material and a very large test suite.

But they were not in TestFlight or the Google Play test track.

The product was largely there. The release was stuck.

There were several branches, red and cancelled CI runs, overlapping pull requests, store requirements, old task records and a long trail of conversations with different coding agents. Each individual session had made sense while I was in it. Looking at the project as a whole had become much harder.

So I tried an experiment.

## Preparing a shared memory

I had used Claude for most of the development. Whenever I explicitly asked the agents to save implementation learnings, decisions and status updates as fragments in Usable, Claude did that well. The same was true when I told it to consult Usable before solving a problem.

The problem was that I had not made this retrieve-and-write-back loop mandatory throughout the development process.

Too much of the work happened without every agent first consulting what the project had already learned and without every completed task writing its new learning back to Usable. Claude followed those instructions when they were given. They simply were not given consistently enough.

That missing discipline helped create the messy end state: useful knowledge was scattered across conversations and worktrees, task statuses had drifted, and some conclusions had become stale as the code moved on.

Before attempting the release endgame, I asked every active Claude agent to record where it had reached and what remained.

That created something important: a durable project memory outside any single conversation, model or coding tool.

Then I asked both Claude and Codex to assess the entire project independently.

## Two independent assessments

The prompt was deliberately broad: inspect the repository, GitHub, CI history and the newest Flowcore project fragments in Usable, then tell me the real state of the project.

Claude and Codex approached the problem differently.

They agreed on the central conclusion. The applications were feature-rich, but the project was not continuously green or ready for store delivery. Several release requirements still lived in unmerged work, and the project records presented a cleaner picture than reality.

But the value was not in the agreement.

It was in what each assessment found that the other missed.

Claude’s audit found two local worktrees containing uncommitted changes that existed nowhere else. A routine cleanup could have destroyed them. It also reconciled stale task statuses, release documentation and the order in which several overlapping pull requests needed to be handled.

Codex challenged the description of the product as “feature-complete.” The task slices might have been completed, but several requirements in the original product specification were still missing or had never been explicitly de-scoped.

It also looked more closely at some production-derived API fixtures. Claude had treated them mainly as a repository-confidentiality concern. Codex traced them into the iOS application’s resource build phase.

That changed the severity completely.

The issue was no longer merely that sensitive fixture data existed in a private repository. A normal iOS archive could potentially include it in the distributed application bundle.

That became a release blocker.

## The useful part was the disagreement

At this point I did not simply choose the assessment I liked best.

I asked Claude to read Codex’s assessment from Usable.

Claude changed several conclusions.

It withdrew the claim that the project was PRD-complete. It accepted Codex’s evidence that most of the changing iOS failures were more consistent with an overloaded CI simulator than with many independent product bugs. That changed the recommendation from chasing tests one by one to sharding the suite while separately investigating the one failure that appeared consistently.

Claude also added findings it had missed, including the absence of required branch protection and the fact that the release workflows had never actually produced and uploaded artifacts.

Then I asked Codex to read Claude’s reconciled assessment.

Codex changed its priorities too.

The stranded worktrees became the first preservation task. The production-derived fixtures became a hard “no release dispatch” gate. A support URL that led unauthenticated users to a login page became a store-readiness problem. Codex refined the integration strategy for the overlapping pull requests instead of treating each one independently.

Neither agent produced the final answer alone.

The useful result emerged through independent inspection, disagreement, verification and write-back.

## From assessment to coordinated work

Codex then converted the reconciled state into a dependency-ordered release programme in Usable Tasks.

The work was no longer a loose checklist. Each task had acceptance criteria, dependencies, verification steps and links back to the project memory that explained why it existed.

And the process has already produced concrete results.

As I write this:

- the two vulnerable worktrees have been preserved as remote branches and draft pull requests, without merging their stale changes;
- the public support page and the association files needed for iOS and Android links are live with unauthenticated access;
- the main correctness repair has been merged;
- the post-merge iOS run produced an honest result instead of being hidden by a timeout: 131 of 132 UI tests passed;
- the remaining failure was narrowed to a test assumption about traversing a lazily rendered settings list, and a focused correction is being verified;
- stale project documentation and task states have been reconciled; and
- two additional store prerequisites—verified Android link coverage and account-deletion handling—have been made explicit rather than being discovered during submission.

The applications are still not in TestFlight or the Google Play test track.

That is the final test of this process, and I do not want to claim the outcome before it exists.

But the collaboration has already moved beyond producing an impressive report. It has preserved work, changed priorities, prevented a potential data exposure, improved the release plan and driven verified implementation.

## What Usable did—and what it did not do

Usable did not reason about the project.

Claude and Codex did that.

Usable also did not replace the repository, GitHub, CI or live service checks. Those remained the sources of current operational truth.

What Usable provided was the durable layer between them:

- a place to record decisions and their reasoning;
- a way to preserve implementation learnings beyond one session;
- a shared project state that different toolsets could retrieve;
- a medium for one agent to challenge and improve another agent’s work;
- and a write-back loop that made the improved conclusion available to the next task.

Claude and Codex never shared a chat or context window. They collaborated asynchronously by reading and updating the same organisational memory.

That distinction matters.

The goal is not to make one enormous conversation that every agent must inhabit. It is to make the relevant learning available wherever the next piece of work happens.

## It was not automatic

There is an important limitation in this story.

The workflow still requires discipline.

Agents need clear instructions to retrieve relevant memory before planning, to distinguish durable learning from temporary status, and to write verified results back after implementation. Without those habits, even a very capable model will solve the problem in front of it and leave much of the value trapped in its session.

The memory also needs maintenance. Old task states and stale summaries can mislead future work if live evidence and newer decisions are not given priority.

So this is not a story about adding a memory tool and watching autonomous collaboration magically emerge.

It is a story about creating an operating system for collaboration:

> inspect current reality → retrieve prior context → decide and execute → verify → write the learning back

Usable makes that loop possible across models and tools. The working discipline makes it reliable.

## The larger lesson

AI models will continue to improve, and the tools around them will keep changing.

An organisation may use Claude for one project, Codex for another and something entirely different six months from now.

If the knowledge remains trapped inside each tool, every change creates another restart.

The models are rented. The organisation’s memory should be owned.

What happened in this project is a small but concrete example. Two toolsets that cannot speak directly were able to build on, test and correct each other’s work because the project’s memory lived somewhere neutral and durable.

The real measure is not whether an agent remembers a conversation.

It is whether the organisation can carry what it learned into the next decision, the next task and the next tool.

I will write a follow-up when the applications reach TestFlight and the Google Play test track—or when the process teaches us something else that changes the conclusion.

For now, the experiment has answered one question for me:

Claude and Codex do not need to share a context window to collaborate.

They need access to the same trustworthy memory.

content.title: Why I am writing here
content.summary: A personal site should be more than a list of roles. This is a place to keep the thinking that happens between the projects.
content.bodyMarkdown:
A list of titles can tell you where someone spends time. It rarely tells you what they are noticing.

I wanted a place for the second part: the ideas that appear while building companies, working with new technology and helping institutions make decisions with consequences beyond the next quarter.

## The work between the work

Most useful lessons do not arrive as polished announcements. They emerge as a changed assumption, a failed experiment, a surprising conversation or a tool that quietly alters how a team thinks. LinkedIn is good for starting a conversation. Product sites are good for explaining a product. Neither is quite the right permanent home for those field notes.

This site is. I will write about durable AI memory, founder work, learning systems, the Faroe Islands, and the practical business of building from a small place with a wide horizon.

## Why Usable CMS

The site also has to practise what I am working on. Its content lives in Usable, where drafts, published versions and the context behind them can remain connected. The public website is still a fast, independent renderer, with a checked-in fallback if the content service is unavailable.

That split matters. Tools should increase your agency without taking your work hostage.

## A working notebook in public

I expect the writing here to be concrete, occasionally unfinished and revised when reality provides a better answer. The promise is not a stream of certainty. It is a useful record of the work and what it teaches.
